Functions of two variables are a vital component in the development of the calculus. Thus, multiple representations of functions are stressed: numerical, symbolic, verbal and graphical. The exponential function is introduced since it is so fundamental to many natural phenomena. Also, the idea of a limit of a function is thoroughly studied, emphasizing the classical tangent and velocity problems -- the study of the derivative. These two quantities are the two most compelling representations of the material covered in this course -- that of the differential calculus. Applications are very much a part of this course. Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. The course concludes with a brief introduction to the second major branch of the calculus: the problem of finding antiderivatives. Course Philosophy: Building on the ideas and techniques of calculus in MATH 1A and MATH 1B, this course introduces students to the application of derivatives and integrals to studying infinite series. Of particular interest is the way in which calculating definite integrals, not possible using elementary techniques, can be approximated using infinite series. Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. At this juncture, students learn to compare and contrast the strengths and weaknesses of the various coordinate systems, and to develop ideas regarding their appropriate usage. Finally, students are introduced to derivatives and integrals of vector functions, and apply these ideas to arc length, curvature, and motion in space. Students are also introduced to parametric equations of curves. Here, students experience for the first time that the ideas of differentiation and integration are not limited to two dimensions, but can be generalized and studied in multi-dimensional format. Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. Course Code: STAT C1000
Title: Introduction to Statistics
Department: Discipline 1 [Mathematics]
Units: 5.0
Prerequisites: Placement as determined by the college’s multiple measures assessment process or completion of a course taught at or above the level of intermediate algebra.
Description: Part 1: This course is an introduction to statistical thinking and processes, including methods and concepts for discovery and decision-making using data. Topics include descriptive statistics; probability and sampling distributions; statistical inference; correlation and linear regression; analysis of variance, chi-squared, and t-tests; and application of technology for statistical analysis including the interpretation of the relevance of the statistical findings. Students apply methods and processes to applications using data from a broad range of disciplines. Part 2: This course is also an introduction to data analysis, making use of graphical and numerical techniques to study patterns and departures from patterns. The student studies randomness with an emphasis on understanding variation collects information in the face of uncertainty, checks distributional assumptions, tests hypotheses, uses probability as a tool for anticipating what the distribution of data may look like under a set of assumptions, and uses appropriate statistical models to draw conclusions from data. The course introduces the student to applications in engineering, business, economics, medicine, education, social sciences, psychology, the sciences, and those pertaining to issues of contemporary interest. The use of technology (computers or graphing calculators) will be required in certain applications. Where appropriate, the contributions to the development of statistics by men and women from diverse cultures will be introduced. This Statistics course is a required lower-division course for students majoring or minoring in many disciplines, such as data science, nursing, business, and others.

Certificates – Overview and Requirements
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza College offers several types of certificates, as described in this section. In general

 
	
Students must complete the required courses as prescribed to earn a certificate.

	
There is no limit on how many certificates a student can earn.

	
Students should check with a counselor and the department offering the desired certificate to get help with planning

Certificates of Achievement and Certificates of Achievement-Advanced

Certificates of Achievement and Certificates of Achievement-Advanced are designed for students interested in instructional
	programs with a high degree of specialization. These academic certificate programs vary in length and generally require
	less than two years of full-time study to complete. If the student prefers, they may be completed on a part-time basis.


Many of these programs have been designed on the ladder concept, so that courses taken to meet requirements for a Certificate
	of Achievement can also count toward some of the requirements for the higher-unit Certificate of Achievement-Advanced, and
	courses required for the Certificate of Achievement-Advanced courses can be applied toward some of the requirements for

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

California Residents

Students who have established California residency for at least one year and a day prior to the term in which they wish to enroll, and have met residency conditions required by state regulations, may enroll as California residents for tuition purposes.

Nonresidents

California residents – and residents of other states or territories – must pay nonresident tuition if they have not resided in California for one year and a day prior to the term in which they wish to enroll.

A unit is the standard measurement of college and university work. One unit equals one hour of classroom work in most classes, predominantly those in lecture or lecture-discussion formats.

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

        units of an audited course for students enrolled in 15 or more quarter units for credit.

No student auditing a course shall be permitted to change his or her enrollment to receive credit for the course.
        Course audits may not be approved to override repetition rules.

        After that, auditors may enroll on a space available basis.

        Instructors have no obligation to grade tests or other class assignments submitted by an auditor; however, an

Course Code: MATH 1A
Title: Calculus I
Department: 
Units: 5.0
Prerequisites: MATH D032., MATH D032H, MATH D043. or MATH D043H (with a grade of C or better), or appropriate score on Calculus Placement Test within the past calendar year
Description: This course covers the fundamentals of differential calculus.
Additional Details:
General Course Statement(s): (See general education pages for the requirements this course meets.)
Transferability: Transferable to both UC and CSU
Advisory(ies): ESL D272. and ESL D273., or ESL D472. and ESL D473., or eligibility for ENGL C1000 or ENGL C1000H or ESL D005.
Limitation(s) on Enrollment: (Not open to students with credit in the Honors Program related course.)
Student Learning Outcomes: Analyze and synthesize the concepts of limits, continuity, and differentiation from a graphical, numerical, analytical and verbal approach, using correct notation and mathematical precision. Evaluate the behavior of graphs in the context of limits, continuity and differentiability. Recognize, diagnose, and decide on the appropriate method for solving applied real world problems in optimization, related rates and numerical approximation.
Course Duration (Weeks): 12.0

Course Philosophy: This is the first course in the calculus sequence. As such, it develops the foundations from which MATH 1B-1D are built. Functions of two variables are a vital component in the development of the calculus. Thus, multiple representations of functions are stressed: numerical, symbolic, verbal and graphical. The exponential function is introduced since it is so fundamental to many natural phenomena. Also, the idea of a limit of a function is thoroughly studied, emphasizing the classical tangent and velocity problems -- the study of the derivative. These two quantities are the two most compelling representations of the material covered in this course -- that of the differential calculus. Applications are very much a part of this course. Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. The course concludes with a brief introduction to the second major branch of the calculus: the problem of finding antiderivatives. This sets the stage for the development of the integral calculus in MATH 1B. This outline contains historical notes relevant to the material covered in the sections they appear. Course Philosophy: This course introduces the problem of finding the area under the graph of a function over an interval-first by approximating the areas of rectangles fitted in the desired region, and then by invoking limits to find the exact area. The two seemingly unrelated problems - one, of finding the slope of the tangent line and two, of finding the area under a curve - are in fact very intimately related, as the student learns, through the fundamental theorem of calculus. In fact, differentiation (MATH 1A) and integration (MATH 1B) are inverse processes. The solution to the area problem is useful in solving other problems. For example, it can be used to find arc length of curves, as well as volume and surface area of certain solids. Additional Details:

Synthesize and apply vectors, polar coordinate system and parametric representations in solving problems in analytic geometry, including motion in space.
Course Duration (Weeks): 12.0

Course Philosophy: Building on the ideas and techniques of calculus in MATH 1A and MATH 1B, this course introduces students to the application of derivatives and integrals to studying infinite series. Of particular interest is the way in which calculating definite integrals, not possible using elementary techniques, can be approximated using infinite series. Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. At this juncture, students learn to compare and contrast the strengths and weaknesses of the various coordinate systems, and to develop ideas regarding their appropriate usage. Finally, students are introduced to derivatives and integrals of vector functions, and apply these ideas to arc length, curvature, and motion in space. Students are also introduced to parametric equations of curves. Here, students experience for the first time that the ideas of differentiation and integration are not limited to two dimensions, but can be generalized and studied in multi-dimensional format. Of particular interest is the way in which calculating definite integrals, not possible using elementary techniques, can be approximated using infinite series. Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. At this juncture, students learn to compare and contrast the strengths and weaknesses of the various coordinate systems, and to develop ideas regarding their appropriate usage. Finally, students are introduced to derivatives and integrals of vector functions, and apply these ideas to arc length, curvature, and motion in space. Students are also introduced to parametric equations of curves. Here, students experience for the first time that the ideas of differentiation and integration are not limited to two dimensions, but can be generalized and studied in multi-dimensional format. A unit is the standard measurement of college and university work. One unit equals one hour of classroom work in most classes, predominantly those in lecture or lecture-discussion formats. 

Students should expect to spend two hours of outside preparation for each one hour spent in class. Laboratory classes have three hours of work per week per unit. (Specialized performance classes such as athletics, drama and music require more than three hours per week per unit.)

Quarter units are equal to two-thirds of a semester unit. Conversely, a semester unit is equal to one and a half quarter units.

Description: Part 1: This course is an introduction to statistical thinking and processes, including methods and concepts for discovery and decision-making using data. Topics include descriptive statistics; probability and sampling distributions; statistical inference; correlation and linear regression; analysis of variance, chi-squared, and t-tests; and application of technology for statistical analysis including the interpretation of the relevance of the statistical findings. Students apply methods and processes to applications using data from a broad range of disciplines. Part 2: This course is also an introduction to data analysis, making use of graphical and numerical techniques to study patterns and departures from patterns. The student studies randomness with an emphasis on understanding variation collects information in the face of uncertainty, checks distributional assumptions, tests hypotheses, uses probability as a tool for anticipating what the distribution of data may look like under a set of assumptions, and uses appropriate statistical models to draw conclusions from data. The course introduces the student to applications in engineering, business, economics, medicine, education, social sciences, psychology, the sciences, and those pertaining to issues of contemporary interest. The use of technology (computers or graphing calculators) will be required in certain applications. Where appropriate, the contributions to the development of statistics by men and women from diverse cultures will be introduced. This Statistics course is a required lower-division course for students majoring or minoring in many disciplines, such as data science, nursing, business, and others.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

De Anza College assigns registration dates based on priority groups, following state and local regulations. These groups are designed to help new students start well and reward continuing students making progress toward their goals.

To qualify for priority registration, students generally need to:
*   Declare a major (not "Undecided").
*   Select a goal of transfer, degree, or certificate.
*   Complete the assessment process.
*   Complete orientation.
*   Create an educational plan (abbreviated for new students, comprehensive for continuing students).

Additionally, to receive priority registration, students cannot have completed more than 150 quarter units in degree-applicable courses (W and I grades, pre-collegiate English, ESL, and Math classes do not count toward this limit).

Here's a general overview of how some priority groups are ordered:

*   **Group 1:** Veterans, foster youth, DSPS, EOPS, CalWorks, student parents (who meet specific criteria), and Rising Scholars students who have completed orientation, assessment, and an educational plan.
*   **Group 2:** Student athletes who have selected an educational goal of transfer, degree or certificate, declared a major, have not been on probation for two consecutive terms, and completed orientation, assessment, and an educational plan.
*   **Continuing Students:** Those who have selected an educational goal of transfer, degree or certificate, and declared a major and have not been on probation for two consecutive terms.

Specific registration dates for these groups vary by quarter. For example, for a recent quarter:
*   Group 1 registration opened on April 27.
*   Group 2 registration opened on April 28.
*   Group 3 registration opened on April 29.

You can register from your assigned start date through the end of the add/drop period. After completing all the necessary steps, allow time for your record to be updated to reflect your priority registration status.

For more detailed information, including specific dates for upcoming quarters and how to register, please visit deanza.edu.

High school students enrolled in grades 9-12, as well as students who are enrolled in eligible adult school programs, may apply to De Anza as special part-time students.

A unit is the standard measurement of college and university work. One unit equals one hour of classroom work in most classes, predominantly those in lecture or lecture-discussion formats.

To apply for the De Anza College Promise, you need to submit the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) or the California Dream Act Application (CADAA) by August 31 and list De Anza College on the application. There is no separate application required for the Promise program itself.

You must also meet the following criteria:
*   Be a first-time college student.
*   Be a California resident or qualify for AB 540 status.
*   Have a household income of less than $200,000 (or below $300,000 according to another source, so it's best to check deanza.edu/promise for the most current information).
*   Apply and enroll in the fall quarter.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Yes, you can take classes at both De Anza and Foothill College at the same time. However, there are a few important things to keep in mind:

*   **Course Families:** If a De Anza course is equivalent to a Foothill course within a designated "course family" (e.g., physical education, visual arts, performing arts), you cannot take both. You are also limited to enrolling no more than six times in courses within a designated course family across both colleges.
*   **Academic Standing:** If you are enrolled at both colleges, you are responsible for monitoring your grades to maintain good standing at each institution. It's possible to be in good standing at Foothill while being on academic or progress notice, or even subject to dismissal, at De Anza if your academic performance at De Anza falls below the required standards. If you have an academic history with both colleges or are enrolled at both during the same quarter, contact your De Anza counselor or the Academic Awareness Program for assistance with your academic or progress notice status.
*   **High School/Adult School Dual Enrollment:** If you are a high school or eligible adult school student taking classes at both colleges, your combined unit total will determine if you are considered full-time and charged enrollment fees. Taking more than 11 units in a regular quarter or more than six units in summer across both colleges will result in being considered full-time and incurring fees.
*   **F or F-1 Visa Students:** If you are attending another college on an F or F-1 visa and wish to take a class at De Anza, you must submit an official letter from your host college. This letter needs to state your standing, confirm your full-time status, and authorize you to take specific De Anza classes.

For more information, you can visit deanza.edu.

Course Philosophy: Building on the ideas and techniques of calculus in MATH 1A and MATH 1B, this course introduces students to the application of derivatives and integrals to studying infinite series. Of particular interest is the way in which calculating definite integrals, not possible using elementary techniques, can be approximated using infinite series. Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. At this juncture, students learn to compare and contrast the strengths and weaknesses of the various coordinate systems, and to develop ideas regarding their appropriate usage. Finally, students are introduced to derivatives and integrals of vector functions, and apply these ideas to arc length, curvature, and motion in space. Students are also introduced to parametric equations of curves. The course introduces the student to applications in engineering, business, economics, medicine, education, social sciences, psychology, the sciences, and those pertaining to issues of contemporary interest. The use of technology (computers or graphing calculators) will be required in certain applications. Where appropriate, the contributions to the development of statistics by men and women from diverse cultures will be introduced. This Statistics course is a required lower-division course for students majoring or minoring in many disciplines, such as data science, nursing, business, and others.

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Students should regularly perform a degree audit through Degree Works to monitor their own progress in reaching educational goals and meeting graduation requirements. It's also recommended that students consult with a counselor or academic adviser.

During the quarter preceding the quarter in which they plan to graduate, students should conduct a detailed review of their completed coursework, and compare the results against the requirements for the desired degree or certificate. google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite.answer:
De Anza College assigns registration dates based on priority groups, in accordance with state and local regulations. These groups are designed to support new students in starting college successfully and to recognize continuing students who are making consistent progress toward their goals.

To qualify for priority registration, students must complete several steps:
*   **Declare a major:** This cannot be "Undecided."
*   **Select a goal:** This must be transfer, degree, or certificate.
*   **Complete the assessment process:** This can be done using U.S. high school transcripts and GPA, or through the Guided Self-Placement tool if you did not attend a U.S. high school recently. More information is available at deanza.edu/assessment.
*   **Complete orientation:** This can be done through a workshop or online. Details are at link.deanza.edu/orientation.
*   **Create an educational plan:** New students develop an abbreviated plan for their first one or two quarters, while continuing students need a comprehensive plan for three or more quarters. This is done through Degree Works on MyPortal. More information is at link.deanza.edu/edplan.

Students generally cannot have completed more than 150 quarter units in degree-applicable courses to receive priority registration. W and I grades, as well as pre-collegiate English, ESL, and Math classes, do not count toward this unit total.

The priority registration order is as follows:
*   **Group 1:** Veterans, foster youth, DSPS, EOPS, CalWorks, student parents, and Rising Scholars students who have completed orientation, assessment, and an educational plan. Student parents are defined as those with one or more children under 18 who receive more than half their support from the student parent.
*   **Group 2:** Student athletes who have selected an educational goal (transfer, degree, or certificate), declared a major, have not been on probation for two consecutive terms, and have completed orientation, assessment, and an educational plan.
*   **Continuing students:** Those who have selected an educational goal (transfer, degree, or certificate) and declared a major, and have not been on probation for two consecutive terms.

For specific registration dates, please refer to the De Anza College calendar at deanza.edu/calendar.

Financial Aid and Scholarships
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
Financial aid is available through the college for students who need financial support to pursue their education. The
    college provides assistance in the form of grants, scholarships, loans and part-time jobs, as well as the De Anza
    College Promise program. Except for scholarships and the De Anza College Promise, all programs require that a
    student show financial need in order to qualify.

Application Procedure

Most students should use the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA), available at  fafsa.gov . Carefully follow the

Units of Academic Credit
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
A unit is the standard measurement of college and university work. One unit equals one hour of classroom work in most classes, predominantly those in lecture or lecture-discussion formats. 

Students should expect to spend two hours of outside preparation for each one hour spent in class. Laboratory classes have three hours of work per week per unit. (Specialized performance classes such as athletics, drama and music require more than three hours per week per unit.)

Quarter units are equal to two-thirds of a semester unit. Conversely, a semester unit is equal to one and a half quarter units.

Students, faculty, staff and community members are welcome to use the center’s resources, which include academic courses, lectures, exhibits, special events and publications.

A key resource at the center is the Stocklmeir Library and Archives, a growing collection of materials on California and on almost every aspect of Santa Clara Valley’s development. A book and journal collection and archives, including student research papers, audio and video oral history, photographs, manuscripts, ephemera, newsletters, clippings and pamphlets are available for research.

*   **Village Centers:** These are physical spaces on campus where you can study, meet with counselors and staff, hang out with friends, and participate in organized activities. They are marked by brightly colored signs and are included on campus maps.
*   **Online:** You can visit your Village's webpage or log in to your Village site on Canvas, the college's online learning platform.

The Villages are part of De Anza's Guided Pathways initiative, which aims to provide students with clear paths and relevant support to achieve their academic goals efficiently. Each Village has a designated Success Team of academic counselors and staff members who offer guidance and support, including program maps that outline plans for obtaining a degree, certificate, or transfer.

Villages host various events throughout the year, such as career panels, transfer panels, guest speakers, workshops, games, and movie days. Weekly "hangouts" also provide opportunities for informal conversation. These events are open to all students, regardless of their Village affiliation.

For more information, you can visit deanza.edu/villages.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Yes, you can take classes at both De Anza and Foothill College at the same time. However, there are some important considerations:

*   **Course Families:** If a course is part of a "course family" (which includes active participation courses like physical education, visual arts, or performing arts), you are limited to enrolling in a total of six courses within that family across both De Anza and Foothill. Each course in these families is nonrepeatable and can only be taken once. If you enroll in a De Anza course that is equivalent to a Foothill course within the same family, you cannot take the Foothill course, and vice versa. More information can be found at deanza.edu/register/repeat-limits and deanza.edu/register/course-families.
*   **Academic Standing:** You are responsible for tracking your grades at both colleges to maintain good standing at each. It's possible to be in good standing at Foothill while being on academic or progress notice at De Anza if your performance falls below De Anza's standards. If you are enrolled at both colleges or have an academic history with both, it's recommended to contact your De Anza counselor or the Academic Awareness Program for assistance.
*   **Dual Enrollment Units:** If you are a high school or eligible adult school student applying for dual enrollment, the total number of units you take at both De Anza and Foothill combined counts towards your enrollment status. Taking more than 11 units in a regular quarter (or more than six in summer) at either or both colleges will result in being charged enrollment fees. For more details, visit deanza.edu/dual.
*   **Residency:** If you are attending another college on an F or F-1 visa, you must submit an official letter from your host college authorizing you to take classes at De Anza. This letter should confirm your full-time status and specify the De Anza classes you are permitted to take.

For more information on residency requirements, visit deanza.edu/admissions/residency.

The main difference between CIS 22A and CIS 22B is the level of programming methodologies in C++ that they cover.

CIS 22A, Beginning Programming Methodologies in C++, covers the fundamental constructs of programming and introduces object-oriented programming. It emphasizes structured procedural programming with an introduction to object-oriented programming.

CIS 22B, Intermediate Programming Methodologies in C++, builds on the foundation established in CIS 22A and covers more advanced topics in object-oriented programming, including strings, multidimensional arrays, pointers, structures, classes, inheritance, polymorphism, templates, exceptions, and linked lists. It also focuses on design, programming style, documentation, testing, and debugging techniques.

In terms of prerequisites, CIS 22B requires CIS 22A as a prerequisite, indicating that CIS 22A is a foundational course and CIS 22B is a more advanced course that assumes prior knowledge of C++ programming.

Overall, CIS 22A is designed to introduce students to programming concepts and C++ basics, while CIS 22B is designed to help students develop more advanced programming skills and knowledge of C++ programming methodologies.

Of particular interest is the way in which calculating definite integrals, not possible using elementary techniques, can be approximated using infinite series. Course Philosophy: This is the first course in the calculus sequence. As such, it develops the foundations from which MATH 1B-1D are built. Functions of two variables are a vital component in the development of the calculus. Thus, multiple representations of functions are stressed: numerical, symbolic, verbal and graphical. The exponential function is introduced since it is so fundamental to many natural phenomena. Also, the idea of a limit of a function is thoroughly studied, emphasizing the classical tangent and velocity problems -- the study of the derivative. These two quantities are the two most compelling representations of the material covered in this course -- that of the differential calculus. Applications are very much a part of this course. Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. The course concludes with a brief introduction to the second major branch of the calculus: the problem of finding antiderivatives. This sets the stage for the development of the integral calculus in MATH 1B. This outline contains historical notes relevant to the material covered in the sections they appear. Course Philosophy: This course introduces the problem of finding the area under the graph of a function over an interval-first by approximating the areas of rectangles fitted in the desired region, and then by invoking limits to find the exact area. The two seemingly unrelated problems - one, of finding the slope of the tangent line and two, of finding the area under a curve - are in fact very intimately related, as the student learns, through the fundamental theorem of calculus. Description: Part 1: This course is an introduction to statistical thinking and processes, including methods and concepts for discovery and decision-making using data. Topics include descriptive statistics; probability and sampling distributions; statistical inference; correlation and linear regression; analysis of variance, chi-squared, and t-tests; and application of technology for statistical analysis including the interpretation of the relevance of the statistical findings. Students apply methods and processes to applications using data from a broad range of disciplines. Part 2: This course is also an introduction to data analysis, making use of graphical and numerical techniques to study patterns and departures from patterns. The student studies randomness with an emphasis on understanding variation collects information in the face of uncertainty, checks distributional assumptions, tests hypotheses, uses probability as a tool for anticipating what the distribution of data may look like under a set of assumptions, and uses appropriate statistical models to draw conclusions from data. The course introduces the student to applications in engineering, business, economics, medicine, education, social sciences, psychology, the sciences, and those pertaining to issues of contemporary interest. The use of technology (computers or graphing calculators) will be required in certain applications. Where appropriate, the contributions to the development of statistics by men and women from diverse cultures will be introduced. This Statistics course is a required lower-division course for students majoring or minoring in many disciplines, such as data science, nursing, business, and others.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Students should regularly perform a degree audit through Degree Works to monitor their own progress in reaching educational goals and meeting graduation requirements. It's also recommended that students consult with a counselor or academic adviser.

During the quarter preceding the quarter in which they plan to graduate, students should conduct a detailed review of their completed coursework, and compare the results against the requirements for the desired degree or certificate. meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct.answer:
To apply to De Anza College, you can follow these simple steps:

1. Go to the De Anza College website at [www.deanza.edu](http://www.deanza.edu) and click on the "Apply Now" button.
2. You will be taken to the OpenCCC online application system, which is used by De Anza and other California community colleges.
3. Fill out the application and submit it. Please allow 7-10 working days for processing.
4. If you haven't received a "welcome" email with your 8-digit student ID number (CWID) after 10 business days, you can email [admissions@deanza.edu](mailto:admissions@deanza.edu) for assistance.

Note: If you are an international student attending on an F-1 visa, or a high school or adult school student seeking dual enrollment, you will need to use a different application form. You can find more information on the De Anza College website under "Special Notes" or by visiting the Admissions and Records Office.

                              connection; it is also that place where that person intends to remain, and during
                              absences intends to return. Residence results from the union of physical presence
                              with objective evidence that the intent is to remain at that place for an indefinite
                              period of time.
Burden of Proof:
The student has the burden of proof to clearly demonstrate both physical presence
                              in California and intent to establish a California residence.
Physical Presence:
A person capable of establishing residence in California must be physically present
                              in California for one year and one day prior to the residence determination date (first
                              day of the term) to be classified as a resident for that term.
Intent:
The law and regulations require both physical presence and the intent of the student

This means you must have been physically present in California and have shown intent to make California your home for an indefinite period of time.

According to the residency requirements, you can demonstrate intent through various means, such as:

If you are under 24 years old and financially supported by a parent or court-appointed legal guardian, you may also need to provide proof of their California residency, such as their tax return with you listed as a dependent.

To get a fee waiver, you can apply for several options available at De Anza College. 

1. **California College Promise (formerly the Board of Governors’ Fee Waiver)**: This waiver is available for eligible students. You can find more information on the De Anza College website.

2. **De Anza College Promise**: This program provides free tuition and fees for eligible first-time college students who are planning to attend full-time. You must be a California resident, have an annual household income below $300,000, and meet other eligibility criteria. You can learn more at deanza.edu/promise.

3. **Fee Waiver for Six or Fewer Units**: If you are a nonresident student taking no more than six units at De Anza and Foothill College, combined, you can apply to have your nonresident tuition waived. You must complete the "Six-Unit Nonresident Fee Waiver" form and meet the eligibility criteria.

4. **Other Fee Waivers**: You can also waive optional fees such as the DASG Membership Fee, Registration Support Fee, and Student Representation Fee by submitting a written request in person or by email to [cashier@deanza.edu](mailto:cashier@deanza.edu) during the registration period.

For more information and to determine which fee waiver you are eligible for, please visit the De Anza College website at deanza.edu or contact the Cashier's Office or Financial Aid Office.

To apply for the De Anza College Promise, follow these steps:

1. **Submit your FAFSA or CADAA**: By August 31, submit the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) or the California Dream Act Application (CADAA) and list De Anza College on the application.
2. **Apply for admission**: If you haven’t already been admitted to De Anza, apply for admission. You must be a California resident (or qualify for AB 540 status) and a first-time college student.
3. **Register for at least 12 units**: Register for at least 12 units per quarter (except summer) to be considered full-time and maintain your eligibility for the De Anza College Promise.

Note: You must meet the eligibility requirements, which include:
- Being a first-time college student
- Having a household income of less than $200,000
- Maintaining full-time status (at least 12 units per quarter) and a 2.0 GPA

For more information and personal assistance, meet with a counselor. You can also visit the De Anza College Promise webpage at [https://www.deanza.edu/promise/](https://www.deanza.edu/promise/) for more details.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

When a student receives a substandard grade (D+, D, D-, F, NC or NP) at De Anza, they may petition to have that grade excluded from their GPA after subsequently completing an equivalent course at another regionally accredited college or university.

Alleviating a substandard grade with a subsequent Pass/No Pass grade is not permitted, as it does not improve the student's GPA. All grades remain on the academic transcript, and some transfer institutions may require recalculation of the GPA to include both the substandard grade and the subsequent grade.

Course Philosophy: This is the first course in the calculus sequence. As such, it develops the foundations from which MATH 1B-1D are built. Functions of two variables are a vital component in the development of the calculus. Thus, multiple representations of functions are stressed: numerical, symbolic, verbal and graphical. The exponential function is introduced since it is so fundamental to many natural phenomena. Also, the idea of a limit of a function is thoroughly studied, emphasizing the classical tangent and velocity problems -- the study of the derivative. These two quantities are the two most compelling representations of the material covered in this course -- that of the differential calculus. Applications are very much a part of this course. Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. The course concludes with a brief introduction to the second major branch of the calculus: the problem of finding antiderivatives. This sets the stage for the development of the integral calculus in MATH 1B. This outline contains historical notes relevant to the material covered in the sections they appear. Course Philosophy: This course introduces the problem of finding the area under the graph of a function over an interval-first by approximating the areas of rectangles fitted in the desired region, and then by invoking limits to find the exact area. The two seemingly unrelated problems - one, of finding the slope of the tangent line and two, of finding the area under a curve - are in fact very intimately related, as the student learns, through the fundamental theorem of calculus. In fact, differentiation (MATH 1A) and integration (MATH 1B) are inverse processes. The solution to the area problem is useful in solving other problems. For example, it can be used to find arc length of curves, as well as volume and surface area of certain solids. At this juncture, students learn to compare and contrast the strengths and weaknesses of the various coordinate systems, and to develop ideas regarding their appropriate usage. Finally, students are introduced to derivatives and integrals of vector functions, and apply these ideas to arc length, curvature, and motion in space. Students are also introduced to parametric equations of curves. Here, students experience for the first time that the ideas of differentiation and integration are not limited to two dimensions, but can be generalized and studied in multi-dimensional format. Students should expect to spend two hours of outside preparation for each one hour spent in class. Laboratory classes have three hours of work per week per unit. (Specialized performance classes such as athletics, drama and music require more than three hours per week per unit.)

Quarter units are equal to two-thirds of a semester unit. Conversely, a semester unit is equal to one and a half quarter units.

Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. Course Philosophy: This course introduces the problem of finding the area under the graph of a function over an interval-first by approximating the areas of rectangles fitted in the desired region, and then by invoking limits to find the exact area. The two seemingly unrelated problems - one, of finding the slope of the tangent line and two, of finding the area under a curve - are in fact very intimately related, as the student learns, through the fundamental theorem of calculus. Course Code: STAT C1000
Title: Introduction to Statistics
Department: Discipline 1 [Mathematics]
Units: 5.0
Prerequisites: Placement as determined by the college’s multiple measures assessment process or completion of a course taught at or above the level of intermediate algebra.
Description: Part 1: This course is an introduction to statistical thinking and processes, including methods and concepts for discovery and decision-making using data. Topics include descriptive statistics; probability and sampling distributions; statistical inference; correlation and linear regression; analysis of variance, chi-squared, and t-tests; and application of technology for statistical analysis including the interpretation of the relevance of the statistical findings. Students apply methods and processes to applications using data from a broad range of disciplines. Part 2: This course is also an introduction to data analysis, making use of graphical and numerical techniques to study patterns and departures from patterns. The student studies randomness with an emphasis on understanding variation collects information in the face of uncertainty, checks distributional assumptions, tests hypotheses, uses probability as a tool for anticipating what the distribution of data may look like under a set of assumptions, and uses appropriate statistical models to draw conclusions from data. The course introduces the student to applications in engineering, business, economics, medicine, education, social sciences, psychology, the sciences, and those pertaining to issues of contemporary interest. The use of technology (computers or graphing calculators) will be required in certain applications. Where appropriate, the contributions to the development of statistics by men and women from diverse cultures will be introduced. This Statistics course is a required lower-division course for students majoring or minoring in many disciplines, such as data science, nursing, business, and others.

Students taking noncredit courses may receive letter grades or be graded on the basis of Pass/No Pass or satisfactory
	progress. (The grading format will be determined by the department; see the course description for more information.) Noncredit
	courses are not recorded on a student’s academic transcript and grades are not calculated in a student’s GPA. (A noncredit

Costs

While noncredit courses are tuition-free, students are responsible for purchasing their own materials and textbooks.

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Here are some important policies regarding California residency for tuition purposes.

California Residents

Students who have established California residency for at least one year and a day prior to the term in which they wish to enroll, and have met residency conditions required by state regulations, may enroll as California residents for tuition purposes.

Nonresidents

California residents – and residents of other states or territories – must pay nonresident tuition if they have not resided in California for one year and a day prior to the term in which they wish to enroll.

Students holding various visas, or undocumented or out-of-status immigrants, may not establish residency and must pay nonresident tuition when enrolling at De Anza. However, nonresidents may be able to establish residency if they meet the requirements of California Education Code § 68062. Others may be exempted from paying nonresident fees through AB 540 eligibility (§ 68130.5), which allows certain nonresident students who have attended a California high school for three years and earned a diploma or equivalent to be charged resident fees. The California History Center is dedicated to promoting the study of local and regional history and encouraging the development of a vibrant civic and cultural life for the community. It has been recognized as an Outstanding Educational Facility by the state of California, while receiving numerous other awards and honors. 

The center is housed in the rehabilitated Trianon building, located on the De Anza College campus and listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Students, faculty, staff and community members are welcome to use the center’s resources, which include academic courses, lectures, exhibits, special events and publications.

A key resource at the center is the Stocklmeir Library and Archives, a growing collection of materials on California and on almost every aspect of Santa Clara Valley’s development. A book and journal collection and archives, including student research papers, audio and video oral history, photographs, manuscripts, ephemera, newsletters, clippings and pamphlets are available for research.

The center also houses the Audrey Edna Butcher Civil Liberties Education Initiative, which engages students and the general public on civil liberties issues.

De Anza is a member of the Coast Conference, the Northern California Football Conference, and the California Community College Athletic Association. History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

With the exception of the Foothill-De Anza district police, campus departments may not hold the DASG card for any reason. Recovered cards should be returned to the Office of College Life immediately.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

If approved, the student's academic transcript will be annotated to reflect exclusion of the previously recorded course with its substandard grade for GPA calculation purposes and for all considerations associated with awarding certificates and degrees. 

Alleviating a substandard grade with a subsequent Pass/No Pass grade is not permitted, as it does not improve the student's GPA. All grades remain on the academic transcript, and some transfer institutions may require recalculation of the GPA to include both the substandard grade and the subsequent grade.

For more information and instructions for submitting a Petition to Replace a Substandard Grade, contact the Admissions and Records Office.

More information:  deanza.edu/admissions

Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. At this juncture, students learn to compare and contrast the strengths and weaknesses of the various coordinate systems, and to develop ideas regarding their appropriate usage. Finally, students are introduced to derivatives and integrals of vector functions, and apply these ideas to arc length, curvature, and motion in space. Students are also introduced to parametric equations of curves. Here, students experience for the first time that the ideas of differentiation and integration are not limited to two dimensions, but can be generalized and studied in multi-dimensional format. A unit is the standard measurement of college and university work. One unit equals one hour of classroom work in most classes, predominantly those in lecture or lecture-discussion formats. 

Students should expect to spend two hours of outside preparation for each one hour spent in class. Laboratory classes have three hours of work per week per unit. (Specialized performance classes such as athletics, drama and music require more than three hours per week per unit.)

Quarter units are equal to two-thirds of a semester unit. Conversely, a semester unit is equal to one and a half quarter units.

Description: Part 1: This course is an introduction to statistical thinking and processes, including methods and concepts for discovery and decision-making using data. Topics include descriptive statistics; probability and sampling distributions; statistical inference; correlation and linear regression; analysis of variance, chi-squared, and t-tests; and application of technology for statistical analysis including the interpretation of the relevance of the statistical findings. Students apply methods and processes to applications using data from a broad range of disciplines. Part 2: This course is also an introduction to data analysis, making use of graphical and numerical techniques to study patterns and departures from patterns. The student studies randomness with an emphasis on understanding variation collects information in the face of uncertainty, checks distributional assumptions, tests hypotheses, uses probability as a tool for anticipating what the distribution of data may look like under a set of assumptions, and uses appropriate statistical models to draw conclusions from data. The course introduces the student to applications in engineering, business, economics, medicine, education, social sciences, psychology, the sciences, and those pertaining to issues of contemporary interest. The use of technology (computers or graphing calculators) will be required in certain applications. Where appropriate, the contributions to the development of statistics by men and women from diverse cultures will be introduced. This Statistics course is a required lower-division course for students majoring or minoring in many disciplines, such as data science, nursing, business, and others.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Here are some important policies regarding California residency for tuition purposes.

California Residents

Students who have established California residency for at least one year and a day prior to the term in which they wish to enroll, and have met residency conditions required by state regulations, may enroll as California residents for tuition purposes.

Nonresidents

California residents – and residents of other states or territories – must pay nonresident tuition if they have not resided in California for one year and a day prior to the term in which they wish to enroll.
