DSPS stands for Disability Support Programs and Services. It is a program designed to ensure that students with disabilities have access to the college's curriculum, facilities, and programs, and to promote their success in achieving their educational and vocational goals. DSPS offers a range of accommodations and services, including but not limited to:

- Readers/Scribes and alternative media requests
- Note-taking accommodations, such as recorded lectures on Canvas
- Extended time on exams
- Interpreting and captioning services

To apply for DSPS, you can follow these steps:

1. Visit the DSPS website at [deanza.edu/dsps/](https://www.deanza.edu/dsps/) for more detailed information and to start the application process.
2. Contact the DSPS office to request an application and to schedule an intake appointment. You can reach them by email at [email protected] or by phone at (408) 864-8838.
3. Provide documentation of your disability as required. This documentation should come from a qualified professional and should outline the nature of your disability and the accommodations you may need.
4. Attend an intake appointment with a DSPS counselor to discuss your needs and develop an individualized accommodation plan.

For more detailed information, you can visit the DSPS website or contact the office directly.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

The Science Resource Center is located in the SC3 building and has a variety of resources – including models, computers, an e-Print kiosk, microscopes, reference books and current textbooks – available for student use outside regular class time.

These resources are used by students and instructors in Biology, Chemistry, Health Technology, Math, Medical Laboratory Technician, Nutrition and Health to supplement class, laboratory and individual study. Students can also sign up to use one of the group study or meeting rooms.

The center supports the principle that learning does not have to stop once a student leaves the classroom; the scientific experience can continue at a time more convenient to the student. While learning is often thought to be a process of the mind, it is heavily influenced by the learner’s environment – the variety of stimuli, the social aspect of the setting, the spatial context, and even the amount of ambient light and sound have all been seen to affect the learning experience. The Science Resource Center is well-suited to the learning experience.

De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Auditing Classes
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
Students who have satisfactorily completed a class for the maximum allowable times may be able to audit a class for
        no credit.

A nonrefundable fee of $10 per unit is assessed for audited classes; however, there is no charge for the first five
        units of an audited course for students enrolled in 15 or more quarter units for credit.

No student auditing a course shall be permitted to change his or her enrollment to receive credit for the course.
        Course audits may not be approved to override repetition rules.

During the first two weeks of class, students enrolling for credit will have registration priority over auditors.
        After that, auditors may enroll on a space available basis.

Auditing carries no privilege other than to attend classes. Students do not receive credit for an audited course.
        Instructors have no obligation to grade tests or other class assignments submitted by an auditor; however, an
        instructor may permit an auditor to participate in class discussions.

Students wishing to audit should contact the instructor. If the instructor approves, they will submit the necessary
        form to the Admissions and Records Office.

qwen/qwen-2.5-72b-instruct.answer:
Yes, you can appeal a grade you disagree with, but there are specific procedures and conditions to follow. According to the California State Administrative Code, the grade given by the instructor is final unless there is evidence of mistake, fraud, bad faith, or incompetency. If you believe your grade should be corrected based on these grounds, you should first discuss the matter with your instructor. If the issue is not resolved, you can proceed with the formal grievance process.

To initiate a formal grievance, you must follow these steps:

1. **Informal Grievance**: Before filing a formal grievance, you must complete the informal grievance process. This typically involves discussing the issue with the instructor and, if necessary, the department chair or division dean.

2. **Formal Griance Form**: If the informal process does not resolve the issue, you can file a formal grievance by submitting the Formal Grievance Form in the Maxient reporting system within 30 days of completing the informal grievance process.

3. **Formal Grievance Submission**: On the form, you will need to specify the rule or law you believe was violated and provide details of the situation. You can also upload any relevant documents.

4. **Acknowledgment**: After submitting the form, you will receive an immediate acknowledgment at the email address you provided.

5. **Grievance Review**: The Grievance Review Board will review your grievance to determine if it meets the standards for filing and further consideration. If the board agrees, a hearing will be scheduled, usually within 30 days of the formal grievance submission.

6. **Hearing**: During the hearing, you and the others involved can be accompanied by, or represented by, any other individual who is not an attorney.

For more detailed information and guidance, you can contact the Office of Student Development or visit the De Anza College website at deanza.edu.

According to De Anza College's policy, to be considered continuously enrolled, you must be enrolled in at least two quarters each academic year at De Anza or Foothill College. Skipping a quarter means you would not meet this requirement, which could potentially change the catalog year used for your degree or certificate evaluation.

For more detailed information, you should refer to the official De Anza College catalog or visit the De Anza College website at deanza.edu.

Course Code: MATH 1A
Title: Calculus I
Department: 
Units: 5.0
Prerequisites: MATH D032., MATH D032H, MATH D043. or MATH D043H (with a grade of C or better), or appropriate score on Calculus Placement Test within the past calendar year
Description: This course covers the fundamentals of differential calculus.
Additional Details:
General Course Statement(s): (See general education pages for the requirements this course meets.)
Transferability: Transferable to both UC and CSU
Advisory(ies): ESL D272. and ESL D273., or ESL D472. and ESL D473., or eligibility for ENGL C1000 or ENGL C1000H or ESL D005.

Student Learning Outcomes: Analyze and synthesize the concepts of limits, continuity, and differentiation from a graphical, numerical, analytical and verbal approach, using correct notation and mathematical precision. Evaluate the behavior of graphs in the context of limits, continuity and differentiability. Recognize, diagnose, and decide on the appropriate method for solving applied real world problems in optimization, related rates and numerical approximation.

Course Philosophy: This is the first course in the calculus sequence. As such, it develops the foundations from which MATH 1B-1D are built. Functions of two variables are a vital component in the development of the calculus. Thus, multiple representations of functions are stressed: numerical, symbolic, verbal and graphical. The exponential function is introduced since it is so fundamental to many natural phenomena. Also, the idea of a limit of a function is thoroughly studied, emphasizing the classical tangent and velocity problems -- the study of the derivative. These two quantities are the two most compelling representations of the material covered in this course -- that of the differential calculus. Applications are very much a part of this course. Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. The course concludes with a brief introduction to the second major branch of the calculus: the problem of finding antiderivatives. This sets the stage for the development of the integral calculus in MATH 1B. This outline contains historical notes relevant to the material covered in the sections they appear. Course Philosophy: This course introduces the problem of finding the area under the graph of a function over an interval-first by approximating the areas of rectangles fitted in the desired region, and then by invoking limits to find the exact area. The two seemingly unrelated problems - one, of finding the slope of the tangent line and two, of finding the area under a curve - are in fact very intimately related, as the student learns, through the fundamental theorem of calculus. In fact, differentiation (MATH 1A) and integration (MATH 1B) are inverse processes. The solution to the area problem is useful in solving other problems. For example, it can be used to find arc length of curves, as well as volume and surface area of certain solids. It has applications in many fields of mathematics, such as, probability and differential equations, as well as other disciplines, such as physics and economics. Course Philosophy: Building on the ideas and techniques of calculus in MATH 1A and MATH 1B, this course introduces students to the application of derivatives and integrals to studying infinite series. Of particular interest is the way in which calculating definite integrals, not possible using elementary techniques, can be approximated using infinite series. Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. At this juncture, students learn to compare and contrast the strengths and weaknesses of the various coordinate systems, and to develop ideas regarding their appropriate usage. Finally, students are introduced to derivatives and integrals of vector functions, and apply these ideas to arc length, curvature, and motion in space. Students are also introduced to parametric equations of curves. Here, students experience for the first time that the ideas of differentiation and integration are not limited to two dimensions, but can be generalized and studied in multi-dimensional format. The exponential function is introduced since it is so fundamental to many natural phenomena. Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. Course Philosophy: Building on the ideas and techniques of calculus in MATH 1A and MATH 1B, this course introduces students to the application of derivatives and integrals to studying infinite series. Of particular interest is the way in which calculating definite integrals, not possible using elementary techniques, can be approximated using infinite series. To apply for an associate degree, students should follow the steps outlined on the Admissions and Records website (deanza.edu/admissions/degrees-certificates). It is recommended to apply before the end of the quarter in which they expect to finish their degree requirements.

For more detailed information on transfer planning, articulation agreements, and course limitations, students can refer to the De Anza College Transfer Guide (deanza.edu/transfer-guide). This guide provides comprehensive information for students planning to transfer to a university.

Please note that the information provided is based on the 2025-2026 academic year, and students should refer to the official De Anza College website for the most up-to-date and accurate information regarding degree requirements and policies.

Course Code: STAT C1000
Title: Introduction to Statistics
Department: Discipline 1 [Mathematics]
Units: 5.0
Prerequisites: Placement as determined by the college’s multiple measures assessment process or completion of a course taught at or above the level of intermediate algebra.
Description: Part 1: This course is an introduction to statistical thinking and processes, including methods and concepts for discovery and decision-making using data. Topics include descriptive statistics; probability and sampling distributions; statistical inference; correlation and linear regression; analysis of variance, chi-squared, and t-tests; and application of technology for statistical analysis including the interpretation of the relevance of the statistical findings. Students apply methods and processes to applications using data from a broad range of disciplines. Part 2: This course is also an introduction to data analysis, making use of graphical and numerical techniques to study patterns and departures from patterns. The student studies randomness with an emphasis on understanding variation collects information in the face of uncertainty, checks distributional assumptions, tests hypotheses, uses probability as a tool for anticipating what the distribution of data may look like under a set of assumptions, and uses appropriate statistical models to draw conclusions from data. The course introduces the student to applications in engineering, business, economics, medicine, education, social sciences, psychology, the sciences, and those pertaining to issues of contemporary interest. The use of technology (computers or graphing calculators) will be required in certain applications. Where appropriate, the contributions to the development of statistics by men and women from diverse cultures will be introduced. This Statistics course is a required lower-division course for students majoring or minoring in many disciplines, such as data science, nursing, business, and others.
Additional Details:
General Course Statement(s): (See general education pages for the requirements this course meets.)
Transferability: Transferable to both UC and CSU
Formerly Statement: (Formerly STAT D010./MATH D010.)
Advisory(ies): ESL D272. and ESL D273., or ESL D472. and ESL D473., or eligibility for ENGL C1000 or ENGL C1000H or ESL D005.
Limitation(s) on Enrollment: (Not open to students with credit in the Honors Program related course.)
Student Learning Outcomes: Organize, analyze, and utilize appropriate methods to draw conclusions based on sample data by constructing and/or evaluating tables, graphs, and numerical measures of characteristics of data. Identify, evaluate, interpret and describe data distributions through the study of sampling distributions and probability theory. Collect data, interpret, compose and evaluate conjectures, and communicate the results of random data using statistical analyses such as interval and point estimates, hypothesis tests, and regression analysis.

The approach that the department has taken in its statistics classes has been motivated by work in the Quantitative Literacy and the Activity Based Statistics projects. Laboratory assignments provide students the opportunity to explore the principles of statistics through the use of technology. Examples and homework problems may be based on real data taken from a variety of contemporary resources, including current articles from the newspaper, web, or other print media. De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

Unit Load Limitations
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
A normal class load is 12-17 units. Students are classified as full-time if they are taking at least 12 units.

New students may not take more than 21.5 units during their first quarter at De Anza without the approval of the dean of Counseling and Disability Support Programs and Services.

Continuing students may enroll in more than 21.5 units (including physical education and labs) if they have met the following conditions:

 
	Completed a minimum of 18 units in the preceding quarter at De Anza

	Have not withdrawn from more than one class in the preceding quarter, and 

	Have a cumulative GPA of at least 3.0

 
Students meeting the above criteria who wish to enroll in more than 21.5 units must petition through their counselor, by meeting with their counselor to complete the Exceeding Units e-form. cohere/command-r-08-2024.answer:
At De Anza College, registration priority groups are assigned based on state and local regulations, ensuring a fair and organized process for students to register for classes. Here's how it works:

**Priority Registration Groups:**
1. **Group 1:** This group includes veterans, foster youth, students with disabilities (DSPS), Educational Opportunity Program (EOPS) participants, and CalWorks students. They must have completed orientation, assessment, and an educational plan to qualify for this group.
2. **Group 2:** Student athletes who have selected an educational goal of transfer, degree, or certificate, declared a major, and not been on probation for two consecutive terms. They also need to complete orientation, assessment, and an educational plan.
3. **Group 3:** Continuing students who have selected an educational goal of transfer, degree, or certificate, declared a major, and not been on probation for two consecutive terms.
4. **Group 4-8:** The remaining groups are assigned registration dates sequentially, with Group 4 opening registration after Group 3, and so on.

**Registration Dates:**
The specific registration dates for each group are subject to change each academic year, so it's essential to refer to the official De Anza College calendar for the most up-to-date information. The calendar provides the opening and continuing registration dates for each group.

**Priority Registration Requirements:**
To qualify for priority registration, students must meet certain criteria:
- Complete orientation, assessment, and an educational plan.
- Declare a major on their application (not "Undecided").
- Select a goal of transfer, degree, or certificate.
- Have not completed more than 150 quarter units in degree-applicable courses (W and I grades are not included).

For more detailed information and the latest updates on priority registration groups and dates, students can refer to the De Anza College website, specifically the "Apply and Register" section, or contact the Admissions and Records Office for assistance.

cohere/command-r-08-2024.answer:
To apply to De Anza College, you can follow these steps:

1. Visit the De Anza College website (deanza.edu) and navigate to the "Apply and Register" section.

2. Click on the "Apply Now" button, which will direct you to the OpenCCC online application system. This system is used by De Anza and other California community colleges.

3. Fill out the online application form. Make sure to declare a major (not "undecided") and select a goal of transfer, degree, or certificate.

4. Submit your application and allow 7-10 working days for processing.

5. If you haven't received a "welcome" email with your 8-digit student ID number (CWID) after 10 business days, contact the Admissions and Records Office at [email protected] Be sure to include your personal details and application information in your email.

6. International students attending on an F-1 visa should use a different application form. Refer to the "Special Notes" section on the De Anza website for more information.

7. High school or adult school students seeking dual enrollment should also refer to the "Special Notes" section for specific instructions.

For any questions or concerns regarding admissions or residency requirements, you can visit the Admission Requirements webpage or contact the Admissions and Records Office for further assistance.

Remember, declaring a major and selecting a goal when filling out the application are important steps to qualify for priority registration.

For more detailed information and guidance, please refer to the De Anza College website or reach out to the Admissions and Records Office for personalized assistance.

The De Anza College Promise program is an initiative designed to make education more accessible and affordable for eligible students. Here's an overview:

**Eligibility:**
- First-time college students
- California residents or those exempted from nonresident tuition (including AB 540 status)
- Household income of less than $200,000
- Full-time enrollment (at least 12 units per quarter)
- Maintain a minimum GPA of 2.0

**Benefits:**
- Free tuition and fees for two years (up to 15 units per quarter)
- Free transportation with the VTA SmartPass

**Application Process:**
- No separate application is required.
- File the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) or the California Dream Act Application (CADAA) by August 31, listing De Anza College.
- Apply and enroll in the fall quarter.

The De Anza College Promise reflects the college's commitment to providing educational opportunities to motivated students regardless of their economic circumstances. For more detailed information and to check your eligibility, visit deanza.edu/promise.

High School and Adult School Admission: Dual Enrollment
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
High school students enrolled in grades 9-12, as well as students who are enrolled in eligible adult school programs, may apply to De Anza as special part-time students.


There is no enrollment fee for current high school students or eligible adult school students who qualify as part-time by taking no more than 11 units during any regular quarter (fall, winter or spring) – or no more than six units in the summer. However, students may still incur costs for textbooks and other fees. Students will be considered full-time – and will be charged enrollment fees and other fees – if they enroll in more than 11 units in a regular quarter, or more than six units in summer, at De Anza College, Foothill College or both colleges combined. Students who want to take more than 11 units in a regular quarter, or more than six units in summer, should contact the Admissions and Records office. More information is available on the website at  deanza.edu/dual .


De Anza recommends that students who are close to earning a high school diploma or GED complete those requirements, when possible, in order to apply and be considered for financial aid when they attend De Anza. Students without a high school diploma are not eligible for federal financial aid.

Based on the provided context, it appears that De Anza College offers a range of financial aid programs to support students in pursuing their education. Here's a summary of the key financial aid options:

- Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA): Students can use the FAFSA to apply for various federal financial aid programs, including the Pell Grant, SEOG (Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant), Student Loans, Cal Grant, and the California College Promise (Fee Waiver).
- California Dream Act Application (CADAA): Undocumented students should use the CADAA instead of the FAFSA to access financial aid opportunities.
- Grants: De Anza College provides grants to students who demonstrate financial need.
- Scholarships: Scholarships are available to students based on academic achievement, leadership, community service, or other criteria.
- Loans: Students can explore loan options to fund their education.
- Part-time Jobs: The college offers part-time job opportunities to eligible students, providing them with financial support and work experience.
- De Anza College Promise Program: This program helps students with financial need by covering enrollment fees and providing additional support. To be eligible, students must maintain a minimum of 12 units each quarter (except summer) and maintain a 2.0 GPA. Students with disability accommodations may have different eligibility requirements.

It's important to note that financial aid applications and deadlines vary, and students are encouraged to visit the De Anza College website (deanza.edu) for detailed information, application forms, and updates. The Financial Aid Office is also available to provide assistance and guidance.

For specific questions regarding financial aid awards, payments, or other academic and support services, students can contact the Financial Aid Office at [email protected] or by calling 408.864.8718.

The California College Promise Grant is a financial aid program that provides tuition coverage for eligible students. To qualify for the California College Promise Grant, you must meet certain criteria:

- Be a California resident or eligible for nonresident tuition exemption.
- Have an annual household income below a certain threshold (as mentioned in the documents, it could be $200,000 or $300,000, depending on the source).
- Be a first-time college student.
- Enroll full-time (at least 12 units per quarter, unless you have a disability accommodation).
- Maintain a minimum GPA of 2.0 to remain eligible.

The California College Promise Grant can provide additional tuition coverage beyond the De Anza College Promise program. When you submit the FAFSA or California Dream Act Application, your financial aid award will list all the aid for which you are eligible, including the California College Promise Grant.

For more detailed information and to determine your eligibility, it's recommended to meet with a counselor or contact the Financial Aid Office at De Anza College. They can provide personalized assistance and guide you through the financial aid process.

You can find more information about financial aid and scholarships at De Anza College by visiting their official website: deanza.edu/promise.

Based on the provided context, here is some information about applying for the De Anza College Promise:

To apply for the De Anza College Promise, you need to meet certain eligibility criteria and follow a few steps:

1. Eligibility:
   - You must be a first-time college student.
   - California resident or qualify for AB 540 status (exempted from nonresident tuition).
   - Have a household income of less than $200,000 (as per Document 2) or $300,000 (as per Document 4).
   - Maintain full-time enrollment (at least 12 units per quarter) and a minimum GPA of 2.0.

2. Application Process:
   - Submit the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) or the California Dream Act Application (CADAA) by August 31. Remember to list De Anza College on your application.
   - Apply for admission to De Anza College if you haven't already been admitted.
   - Register for at least 12 units each quarter (except summer) to maintain full-time status and eligibility for the Promise.
   - The Promise award covers up to 15 units per quarter. You are responsible for any additional units.
   - Non-enrollment fees, such as materials and health costs, are not covered by the Promise.

For more detailed information and personal assistance, it is recommended to meet with a counselor at De Anza College. They can provide guidance and support throughout the application process.

Please refer to the official De Anza College website (deanza.edu) for the most up-to-date and comprehensive information regarding the De Anza College Promise and financial aid programs.

The California History Center is dedicated to promoting the study of local and regional history and encouraging the development of a vibrant civic and cultural life for the community. The center is housed in the rehabilitated Trianon building, located on the De Anza College campus and listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Students, faculty, staff and community members are welcome to use the center’s resources, which include academic courses, lectures, exhibits, special events and publications.

A key resource at the center is the Stocklmeir Library and Archives, a growing collection of materials on California and on almost every aspect of Santa Clara Valley’s development. A book and journal collection and archives, including student research papers, audio and video oral history, photographs, manuscripts, ephemera, newsletters, clippings and pamphlets are available for research.

The Villages at De Anza College are communities that bring together students, faculty, and staff with shared academic interests and related majors. There are six Villages in total, each with its own focus: Artistic Expression, Business and Finance, Health and Life Sciences, Language and Communication, Physical Sciences and Technology, and Social Sciences and Humanities.

Students are encouraged to join a Village to enhance their educational experience and receive relevant support. Each Village has a designated Success Team, consisting of academic counselors and staff, who provide guidance and support tailored to the specific interests and goals of the students within that Village.

The Villages offer a range of resources and activities, including career panels, transfer panels, guest speakers, workshops, games, and movie days. These events are open to all students and provide opportunities for connection, learning, and exploration.

To engage with their Village community, students can visit the designated Village Centers on campus, which are marked with colorful signs and included on campus maps. Alternatively, they can access their Village's online presence through their Village webpage or the Canvas learning platform.

The Villages are part of De Anza's Guided Pathways initiative, which aims to provide clear paths and relevant support for students to achieve their academic goals efficiently. By joining a Village, students can benefit from a supportive network, access to specialized resources, and personalized guidance from their Success Team.

For more detailed information about the Villages and their specific offerings, students can visit the De Anza website at deanza.edu/villages.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

cohere/command-r-08-2024.question: Can I retake a class I already passed to improve my GPA?
cohere/command-r-08-2024.context:
[Document 1] (Source: 2025-2026/repeating-courses):
page 
         06 
          
          
          
          
    
    
        
            
Repeating Courses
        
    
    
    
    
        
            
    
California law limits the number of times you may take the same class at a community college. (See Title 5 § 55024,
    55040, 55042, 55045 and 58161.)

You may repeat a course for which you have earned a substandard grade (such as F, D or NP) or a W. However, you may
    not enroll in the same course more than a total of three times, including times when you received a substandard
    grade or W. If you get a W or substandard grade in the same course twice, you will not be able to enroll in the
    course again until you contact the Admissions and Records office and obtain clearance for taking the course a third
    time.

If you repeat a course because of a W or substandard grade, the second grade will replace the first in calculating
    your GPA, but the initial course and grade will remain on the permanent record. If you take the class for a third

Additional Details:

Student Learning Outcomes: Analyze the definite integral from a graphical, numerical, analytical, and verbal approach, using correct notation and mathematical precision. Course Duration (Weeks): 12.0
Lecture: 60.0
Laboratory: 0.0

Course Philosophy: This course introduces the problem of finding the area under the graph of a function over an interval-first by approximating the areas of rectangles fitted in the desired region, and then by invoking limits to find the exact area. The two seemingly unrelated problems - one, of finding the slope of the tangent line and two, of finding the area under a curve - are in fact very intimately related, as the student learns, through the fundamental theorem of calculus. In fact, differentiation (MATH 1A) and integration (MATH 1B) are inverse processes. The solution to the area problem is useful in solving other problems. For example, it can be used to find arc length of curves, as well as volume and surface area of certain solids. It has applications in many fields of mathematics, such as, probability and differential equations, as well as other disciplines, such as physics and economics. Description: This course covers the fundamentals of differential calculus.
Additional Details:
General Course Statement(s): (See general education pages for the requirements this course meets.)
Transferability: Transferable to both UC and CSU
Advisory(ies): ESL D272. and ESL D273., or ESL D472. and ESL D473., or eligibility for ENGL C1000 or ENGL C1000H or ESL D005.

Student Learning Outcomes: Analyze and synthesize the concepts of limits, continuity, and differentiation from a graphical, numerical, analytical and verbal approach, using correct notation and mathematical precision. Evaluate the behavior of graphs in the context of limits, continuity and differentiability. Recognize, diagnose, and decide on the appropriate method for solving applied real world problems in optimization, related rates and numerical approximation.
Course Duration (Weeks): 12.0
Lecture: 60.0
Laboratory: 0.0
Total: 60.0
Course Credit Status: Credit - Degree Applicable
Effective Term: Fall 2025
Does the course have a Foothill equivalent?: No
Course Philosophy: This is the first course in the calculus sequence. As such, it develops the foundations from which MATH 1B-1D are built. Functions of two variables are a vital component in the development of the calculus. Thus, multiple representations of functions are stressed: numerical, symbolic, verbal and graphical. The exponential function is introduced since it is so fundamental to many natural phenomena. Also, the idea of a limit of a function is thoroughly studied, emphasizing the classical tangent and velocity problems -- the study of the derivative. These two quantities are the two most compelling representations of the material covered in this course -- that of the differential calculus. Applications are very much a part of this course. Problems pertaining to the graphing of functions, related rates, and minimum and maximum are studied. The course concludes with a brief introduction to the second major branch of the calculus: the problem of finding antiderivatives. This sets the stage for the development of the integral calculus in MATH 1B. This outline contains historical notes relevant to the material covered in the sections they appear. Course Code: MATH 1C
Title: Calculus III
Department: 
Units: 5.0
Prerequisites: MATH D001B or MATH D01BH (with a grade of C or better) or equivalent
Description: Students in this course will learn about infinite series, lines, and planes in three dimensions, vectors in two and three dimensions, parametric equations of curves, derivatives, and integrals of vector functions.
Additional Details:
General Course Statement(s): (See general education pages for the requirements this course meets.)
Transferability: Transferable to both UC and CSU
Advisory(ies): ESL D272. and ESL D273., or ESL D472. and ESL D473., or eligibility for ENGL C1000 or ENGL C1000H or ESL D005.
Limitation(s) on Enrollment: (Not open to students with credit in the Honors Program related course.)
Student Learning Outcomes: Analyze infinite sequences and series from the perspective of convergence, using correct notation and mathematical precision. Apply infinite sequences and series in approximating functions. Synthesize and apply vectors, polar coordinate system and parametric representations in solving problems in analytic geometry, including motion in space.
Course Duration (Weeks): 12.0
Lecture: 60.0
Laboratory: 0.0
Total: 60.0
Course Credit Status: Credit - Degree Applicable
Effective Term: Fall 2025
Does the course have a Foothill equivalent?: No
Course Philosophy: Building on the ideas and techniques of calculus in MATH 1A and MATH 1B, this course introduces students to the application of derivatives and integrals to studying infinite series. Of particular interest is the way in which calculating definite integrals, not possible using elementary techniques, can be approximated using infinite series. Students are then introduced to lines, planes and vectors in three dimensions as well as alternate coordinate systems for representing them. At this juncture, students learn to compare and contrast the strengths and weaknesses of the various coordinate systems, and to develop ideas regarding their appropriate usage. Finally, students are introduced to derivatives and integrals of vector functions, and apply these ideas to arc length, curvature, and motion in space. Students are also introduced to parametric equations of curves. Here, students experience for the first time that the ideas of differentiation and integration are not limited to two dimensions, but can be generalized and studied in multi-dimensional format. De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. Guiding principles for the new college called for creating an “open door” institution to serve students with a wide variety of abilities, aptitudes and interests; an atmosphere of “friendly informality between faculty members and students”; and a campus that conveyed a sense of “quiet dignity” and “higher learning.”


Over the decades, De Anza’s enrollment has grown from 3,000 students in its first year to nearly 18,000 today.

microsoft/phi-4.answer:
Based on the provided context, De Anza College assigns registration priority groups to students in accordance with state and local regulations. Here's a summary of how these groups work:

1. **Priority Registration Groups**: Students are assigned registration dates based on specific groups, which are determined by their status and completion of certain requirements. The groups are as follows:

   - **Group 1**: Includes veterans, foster youth, DSPS, EOPS, CalWorks students, and student parents who have completed orientation, assessment, and an educational plan. Student parents must also have one or more children under age 18 who receive more than half their support from the student parent.
   
   - **Group 2**: Includes student athletes, MESA (Mathematics, Engineering, Science Achievement) students, and continuing students who have selected an educational goal of transfer, degree, or certificate, declared a major, and have not been on probation for two consecutive terms. They must also have completed orientation, assessment, and an educational plan.
   
   - **Group 3 to Group 8**: These groups open registration sequentially, with specific dates provided for each group.

2. **Requirements for Priority Registration**: To qualify for priority registration, students must complete several steps:
   - Complete orientation.
   - Complete the assessment process.
   - Create an educational plan through Degree Works.
   - For new students, this plan should cover the first one or two quarters, while continuing students should have a comprehensive plan for three or more quarters.
   - Students must also declare a major on their application and select a goal of transfer, degree, or certificate.

3. **Registration Deadlines**: Each group has specific registration opening and closing dates. It's important for students to register within their assigned group dates to secure their class schedules.

For more detailed information or specific questions, students are directed to visit [De Anza College's official website](https://www.deanza.edu/).

   - Students need to maintain eligibility for aid by meeting academic progress requirements and other conditions.

   - Students can contact the financial aid office for more information or assistance. Virtual office hours are available via Zoom, and in-person assistance is provided at the Baldwin Winery Building.

5. **Additional Resources**:

To apply for the De Anza College Promise, follow these steps:

1. **Submit the FAFSA or CADAA**: File the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) or the California Dream Act Application (CADAA) by August 31. Make sure to list De Anza College on your application. Remember, you need to re-submit every year.

2. **Apply for Admission**: If you haven't already been admitted to De Anza College, you must apply. You must be a California resident or qualify for AB 540 status and be a first-time college student in your first or second year to be eligible for the De Anza College Promise.

3. **Register for Units**: Enroll in at least 12 units each quarter (except summer) to be considered "full time" and maintain your eligibility for the De Anza College Promise. The Promise award will cover up to 15 units per quarter. You are responsible for the cost of any additional units.

For more detailed information or personal assistance, it's recommended to meet with a counselor. For further details, you can visit [De Anza College's Promise page](https://www.deanza.edu/promise/).

The center is housed in the rehabilitated Trianon building, located on the De Anza College campus and listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Students, faculty, staff and community members are welcome to use the center’s resources, which include academic courses, lectures, exhibits, special events and publications.

A key resource at the center is the Stocklmeir Library and Archives, a growing collection of materials on California and on almost every aspect of Santa Clara Valley’s development. A book and journal collection and archives, including student research papers, audio and video oral history, photographs, manuscripts, ephemera, newsletters, clippings and pamphlets are available for research.

History of De Anza College
        
    
    
    
    
        
             
        
    
    
    
        
            
    
De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Planning for the new college began soon after the district’s first campus, Foothill College, launched in temporary quarters in 1958 and filled to capacity after moving in 1961 to its permanent location in Los Altos Hills. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million. De Anza was established in Cupertino on Sept. 11, 1967, as the Foothill Junior College District worked to meet local community demand for a second campus. Just four years after approving a $10.4 million bond measure for Foothill, community members readily voted in favor of a second bond measure, in the amount of $14 million, to build De Anza College.


De Anza was constructed on 112 acres of what was once a turn-of-the-century wine producing estate that the district purchased for $1.1 million.
